Juan Soto Joins Elite Club With 270 Homers, 100 Stolen Bases Before 28th Birthday
New York Mets outfielder Juan Soto just became the fourth player in MLB history to hit 270 home runs and steal 100 bases before his 28th birthday. Friday night, the…
Juan Soto of the New York Mets hits a double in the second inning against the Philadelphia Phillies at Citi Field on September 18, 2026 in New York City.
Photo by Evan Bernstein/Getty Images
New York Mets outfielder Juan Soto just became the fourth player in MLB history to hit 270 home runs and steal 100 bases before his 28th birthday. Friday night, the 27-year-old crushed a 428-foot three-run blast against the Philadelphia Phillies.
Who else made this list? Alex Rodriguez, Ken Griffey Jr., and Mike Trout, per MLB's Sarah Langs. Every player in this group debuted at 19.
According to Essentially Sports, Soto went 3-for-5 with one homer, 3 RBIs, and a run scored against Philadelphia. He's up to 26 homers in 103 games despite missing time on the injured list twice this year.
The five-time All-Star needed 1,199 MLB games to reach 270 home runs. He's also collected 210 doubles as part of his 1,187 hits.
The Dominican star has swiped 104 bases in 134 tries. Last season, he stole 38 bags—a massive jump from his previous career-high of just 12. This year he's 9-for-12 on the basepaths.
Soto draws walks like few others can. He's led MLB in walks four times and has six seasons with at least 100 free passes. Career totals? 969 walks versus only 893 strikeouts. Among active players, he leads everyone with a .415 on-base percentage.
New York inked the outfielder as a free agent before the 2025 season. His contract: 15 years, $765 million. That's the biggest deal in MLB history.
The Mets sit in last place in the NL East at 70-84. Many experts predicted they'd contend for the division title this year. They haven't.
Soto's still producing. He's batting .274 with a .920 OPS across 444 plate appearances in 103 games. His season started late on April 22 after he recovered from a right calf strain. Then he hit the IL again in late July with a left calf strain. He earned his fifth All-Star selection this season but didn't play in the game.

item.content:encoded:
What to watch for as the playoffs loom: Phillies counting on Alex McFarlane, starters as relievers, and more
With their magic number down to three, a fifth straight postseason is in sight for the Phillies. But there are plenty of questions going into the final homestand of the regular season.
The Phillies returned from their final road trip of the season with work to do.
Their magic number to clinch a postseason berth is three. Any combination of wins and Diamondbacks losses that totals three will ensure the Phillies’ season continues beyond Sunday. But while they remain in control of their own destiny, it won’t be easy.
To close out the final week, the Phillies host the top team in the National League in the Brewers, followed by the top team in the American League in the Rays.
Here are a few takeaways heading into the last homestand of the regular season:
Multi-inning McFarlane
The circle of trust in the Phillies bullpen right now is extremely small. The relief unit has a 5.50 ERA in September, and the club took the drastic measure of optioning Orion Kerkering to triple-A Lehigh Valley on Sunday after his struggles became untenable. Unless there is an injury to another member of the staff, he is ineligible to be on the wild-card roster.
While the Phillies’ rotation and closer Jhoan Duran are among the best in the sport, it’s the bridge between them that has been the biggest issue. The Phillies continue to hope Jonathan Bowlan (groin) will be available for the postseason. The right-hander began playing catch Sunday, and reported to the field on Monday’s off day to continue his progress.
Before the injury, Bowlan had been going through a rough stretch, having allowed a run in five of his last six appearances. Even if he were a full go, it would be hard to imagine tossing him right back into an eighth-inning, high-leverage role after spending some time on the shelf.
» READ MORE: Phillies send struggling reliever Orion Kerkering to triple A
Enter Alex McFarlane.
The 25-year-old rookie came through in a big spot against the Mets on Sunday, facing two tough opponents in Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto to get out of a seventh-inning jam. By retiring both of them, McFarlane added a few more notches to his belt, which already included such stars as Shohei Ohtani, Mike Trout, and Nolan Arenado.
But Sunday’s win over the Mets also revealed how interim manager Don Mattingly is planning to handle his relievers in the postseason. After McFarlane struck out Soto to preserve a two-run lead with his 18th pitch, there was initially no movement in the Phillies’ bullpen during the eighth. When the Phillies loaded the bases, that’s when Chase Shugart started getting ready.
Had the Phillies’ lead stayed at two, though, Mattingly was going to send McFarlane back out. Duran would have then started warming to relieve him, and then finish it off in the ninth.
It didn’t wind up happening, but Mattingly envisions using McFarlane and Duran to cover the last nine outs of a close game.
“I think it is [realistic] this time of year,” Mattingly said. “I mean, I think with Jho, you also get to the point where he’s capable of two innings. You’re just trying to get the guys that we need in the game, for as much as you can.”
So while the lack of relief depth is still a concern, things will operate a bit differently in the playoffs. The trusted high-leverage arms, as few as they are, can and will be called upon to do more.
» READ MORE: Don Mattingly thinks Chase Shugart can take on a bigger role in Phillies' bullpen
McFarlane has thrown more than one inning just once in the two months he’s been in the majors, covering 1⅓ innings Aug. 15 against the Twins. He said he is ready to do whatever he’s asked.
“Just grateful for the opportunity,” McFarlane said. “Whatever opportunity he gives me, I’m just gonna take it one game at a time. Make sure I prepare my best, and just give all I can anytime he sends me out there.”
Starters in relief
The Phillies still haven’t mapped out how they will deploy their rotation in a wild-card series. That’s because there are a lot of unknowns: whether they will make it at all, who they will play if they do, and the health of Jesús Luzardo.
The club is “very optimistic” about Luzardo’s progress from the shoulder inflammation that landed him on the injured list, according to president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski. Like Bowlan, he has also progressed to playing catch.
Should Luzardo remain on track to return in time for the postseason, Dombrowski said the Phillies are keeping their options open with how they deploy him. It could be as a starter, which might be a risk given his last outing will have been Sept. 7. It could also be as a reliever, a role Luzardo has less experience in, but experience nonetheless. In the deciding Game 4 of the 2025 National League Division Series, he held off the Dodgers for 1⅔ innings of emergency relief in extras, pitching on short rest.
» READ MORE: The Zack Wheeler conversation: Why he ‘expected’ to thrive after surgery, and how much longer he wants to play
His performance in that role was largely overshadowed by how the game ended, with Kerkering botching a bases-loaded grounder to allow Los Angeles to walk it off. Had Kerkering made the throw to end the inning and things turned out differently, Luzardo’s clutch bullpen appearance might have gone down as legendary instead.
Whether or not Luzardo is one of them, the Phillies bullpen will be getting reinforcements by way of the rotation for the postseason. The question is who.
“Some of our starters are going to end up in the bullpen,” Dombrowski said. “I don’t know how it’s going to work at this point, but some of them will, especially when you get to the first round. We’re going to be the best-of-three, so you only can start three guys at that point. So you got two other guys that can go into the bullpen.”
It’s difficult to see a world where Zack Wheeler or Cristopher Sánchez aren’t starting two of the wild-card games. Aaron Nola has continued his second-half resurgence with a 2.15 ERA since Aug. 3, but he has never been a reliever in any capacity during his major league career, regular season or postseason.
Rookie Andrew Painter continues to be under consideration for making the move. He gave up four runs in his last start against the Mets, but the quality of his stuff remained high. Painter’s first inning especially stood out, when he got Lindor to ground out before striking out Soto and Bo Bichette.
Painter touched 99.4 mph with his fastball in the fifth inning. In a shorter stint, it isn’t hard to imagine him getting into the triple digits.
“I think his stuff will be very solid out there,” Dombrowski said.
» READ MORE: Andrew Painter’s potential role on a Phillies playoff staff is uncertain. Painter says any role is OK with him.
If the opportunity arises in the final six games, Mattingly said he could see the Phillies test-driving that theory by trying Painter out in the bullpen ahead of the playoffs. That said, time is running out.
Painter doesn’t think he necessarily needs a trial run to feel comfortable pitching in relief, however. He has experience with his routine shifting already, pitching behind an opener earlier this year and also appearing in relief after being scratched from his start because of a migraine.
“I feel like postseason baseball, in that atmosphere, the adrenaline is going to be flowing,” Painter said. “I don’t really think there’s much of an adjustment that’s going to be there. I think the adrenaline would just take over from that point.”
More patience from Turner
Whether the Phillies’ offense will get hot at the right time or slide back into a familiar October slumber remains to be seen. But there were some positive signs, particularly from the top of their order, in the series against the Mets.
En route to the series split, it was the top half of the order that carried a lot of the load — excluding a key bases-loaded triple from nine-hole hitter Justin Crawford on Sunday. And that’s how it will need to be for the Phillies to make a deep run.
They didn’t do it with the long ball, as the Phillies’ only two home runs in the series came from Derek Hill and Edmundo Sosa. Instead, they got on base, moved runners, and strung together hits.
Trea Turner in particular had a strong series. He finished 4-for-13 (.308), but the real eye-popping stat was his .526 on-base percentage.
» READ MORE: Can Trea Turner rescue his season despite career-worst stats at the plate? His manager and teammates believe so.
If he could maintain some of that momentum, it would be transformative for the Phillies. What has been a disappointing season by most measures for Turner could be rescued with a strong postseason performance.
“I think more and more, you see how they’re pitching him, and it’s I think basically not throwing him strikes,” Mattingly said of Turner.
According to StatCast, 53.6% of the pitches Turner has seen this year are out of the strike zone. It’s a few percentage points higher than the 51.3% out-of-zone pitches he saw last year, and trails only Kyle Schwarber (54.8%) and Bryce Harper (57.4%) among Turner’s teammates.
The difference has been that Turner swings at those out-of-zone pitches at a much higher clip. His chase rate this year is 34.6%, the second-highest of his career.
But against the Mets, he showed a glimpse of what he could be if he homes in on his selectivity. Turner drew six walks in the four-game series. He also scored three runs.
“The more he walks, the more they’re forced in the strike zone,” Mattingly said. “And when he’s on base, obviously it creates a danger there with him running and things like that. We need him to get on base. When he’s on base, we’re better.”

item.content:encoded:
The playoffs technically don't start for another week or so, but good luck telling that to teams for which every game already feels like October. With the standings in both the NL and AL as jumbled as they've been in recent memory, the stakes are already as high as can be — and whoever gets hot now could well ride that wave all the way to a World Series.
"Hot" could definitely describe both the San Diego Padres and Cleveland Guardians of late. The former has decided to just never lose again, not only grabbing hold of a Wild Card spot but now pushing for home-field in the first round if things break right. The latter, meanwhile, has once again snatched the AL Central while no one was looking. And they're not the only ones making serious moves in our latest MLB power rankings.
But who are we buying as serious title contenders, and who still has work to do? Read on to find out.
30. Colorado Rockies
The Rockies have admittedly let go of the rope of late, well on their way to yet another 100-loss season. There are at least some promising young hitters in this organization, which represents something to build upon moving forward. Of course, the pitching staff remains a mess, and no one's been able to crack that nut yet in Colorado.
–Chris Landers, FanSided.com editor
29. Los Angeles Angels
In Reid Detmers, Walbert Urena and Ryan Johnson, the Angels have at least some sort of foundation upon which to build for the future. Well, OK, maybe not Detmers, who will almost certainly be dealt this offseason. But still, L.A.’s pitching staff has been a real bright spot of late. The offense … well, that’s another question. Things are going to get worse before they get better under John Mozeliak. At least Arte Moreno is no longer around to meddle in it.
–CL
28. Athletics
The A’s are playing out the string of a lost season, although the contributions they’ve gotten from young bats like Henry Bolte, Max Muncy (not that one), Lawrence Butler and Zack Gelof down the stretch have been notable. None of that will matter, though, until the team fixes its pitching staff. We know we sound like a broken record, but it really is that simple, and no potential answers have emerged in the second half.
–CL
27. San Francisco Giants
Rafael Devers' injury, which figures to cost him at least some of next season as well as the end of this one, is a fitting if unfortunate end to what's been a miserable season by the Bay. Devers had been one of the few bright spots on this Giants team down the stretch alongside Bryce Eldridge; now, it's unclear how San Francisco will rebuilt its offense for 2027 in addition to finding reinforcements for a pitching staff that simply hasn't been good enough.
–CL
26. Kansas City Royals
The Kansas City Royals have been eliminated for quite some time now. If there is one clear goal for Kansas City this winter, it's to build a roster around Bobby Witt Jr. that is capable of making a postseason run. That is every team's goal, but the Royals are so far away from contention despite featuring such a prolific player, Witt Jr.'s career is closer to becoming Mike Trout's than Derek Jeter's.
-Mark Powell, FanSided.com MLB director
25. Minnesota Twins
At one point not all that long ago, the Twins had a realistic chance to make the playoffs as the third AL Wild Card spot. Then, the bottom fell out. Byron Buxton underwent successful hip surgery just last week that will keep him out until spring training, whenever that may be. The Twins once again experienced the roster flaw of building around an injured star.
-MP
24. New York Mets
This week couldn’t have been more awkward for the New York Mets when Pete Alonso hit his 300th home run in his return to Citi Field, much to the delight of many Mets fans in attendance, but once Alonso left town, the Mets began to play better, winning two games in a row against the Phillies. Those wins, headlined by more quality play from youngsters like Carson Benge, Zac Thornton and Christian Scott, show why Mets fans should be somewhat enthusiastic for what’s to come.
–Zach Rotman, FanSided.com staff writer
23. Cincinnati Reds
In the American League, the Reds likely wouldn't be the worst team in their division. But the NL Central has been a gauntlet all year long, and the Reds couldn't keep up. Despite breakthrough seasons from Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart, Cincinnati still has a long way to go on the starting pitching front. Can they rely on Hunter Greene and Chase Burns moving forward?
-MP
22. Seattle Mariners
Going 3-3 against the Angels and Rockies this week just about sums up this season in Seattle. The good news is that youngsters like Michael Arroyo and Lazaro Montes have helped to key an offensive turnaround. The bad news is that the starting rotation hasn’t held up its end of the bargain of late, and there are still tons of long-term questions about this lineup — especially with Randy Arozarena set to hit free agency. Jerry DiPoto will need to find some answers this offseason after a year in which just about everything went wrong.
–CL
21. Washington Nationals
The Washington Nationals deserved a better fate in 2026. Even with their offense falling off a bit of late, they’re still third in the majors in runs scored. The dynamic duo of CJ Abrams and James Wood is as good as any in the National League. Recently extended Cade Cavalli is a budding ace. Andrew Alvarez has thrown the ball incredibly well and looks like a future rotation stalwart. If it weren’t for a historically bad bullpen, we’d be talking about this team in Wild Card contention.
–ZR
20. Detroit Tigers
The Tigers have the best run differential in the AL Central and a pythagorean record of an AL playoff team. None of it matters. Scott Harris and the Tigers front office gave up on their team's postseason hopes at the trade deadline. Then, they proceeded to get fans' hopes up with a late August run, only to play like the team Harris assumed they'd become when it mattered most. The Tigers have some work to do, though the emergence of young stars in the lineup like Hao-Yu Lee and Kevin McGonigle, paired with Riley Greene's consistent play, give them some building blocks.
-MP
19. St. Louis Cardinals
The Cardinals are ahead of schedule, but not a postseason team. Make no mistake about it, St. Louis came crashing back down to earth in September, and has been eliminated from playoff contention. There are questions about the long-term future of Masyn Winn, especially with JJ Wetherholt as the de-facto shortstop of the future. But these are all good problems to have. Now, if only Bloom could find an ace burried in that farm system of his.
-MP
18. Baltimore Orioles
A series against league-best Milwaukee came at the worst possible time for the O’s, which now find themselves needing to hit an inside straight to snatch the final Wild Card spot. Pete Alonso’s heroics at Citi Field aside, Baltimore’s bats simply have not been good enough. Heck, no part of this team has; they’re hovering around .500 for a reason, after all, and there’s no reason to think they have the consistency required to get hot over the final week and overtake the White Sox, Blue Jays and Astros.
–CL
17. Miami Marlins
The Miami Marlins tried to do what they could to stick around in the NL postseason hunt, even using Sandy Alcantara on one day of rest in a save opportunity, but they were eliminated following Friday’s loss in San Diego. As disappointing as that is, the Marlins could finish above .500 for just the third time since 2009. That’s a sign that things are heading in the right direction for Miami.
–ZR
16. Toronto Blue Jays
The Jays have lost three of four series now, and news that Dylan Cease will have his next start bumped due to shoulder fatigue makes it even less likely that Toronto can sneak its way into the playoffs. With Trey Yesavage and Shane Bieber already on the IL, the rotation has begun leaking oil, and that’s not something this power-starved lineup is equipped to handle. The Jays still have a path to the final Wild Card spot, but it’s becoming an increasingly tenuous one, and it’s hard to see them making much noise even if they did get in.
–CL
15. Houston Astros
Getting swept at home by the Braves this weekend might well wind up costing the Astros a playoff spot. The closing schedule isn’t too tough, with trips to Seattle and Sacramento on tap. Still, if Houston doesn’t figure out where its high-powered offense went before it’s too late — and if Joe Espada can’t stop his bullpen from blowing late leads — Yordan Alvarez’s MVP season may well be for nought. As it stands, this looks like a team with fatal flaws that will spoil what could have been a deep run in a wide-open AL.
–CL
14. Chicago White Sox
Reality hit the White Sox real quick. Chicago has lingered around .500 for longer than they'd care to admit, and it was only a matter of time before the rest of the Central caught up to them. Munetaka Murakami has been dreadful since the trade deadline, and thus any contract extension talks have been put on hold. If the White Sox can hold on to a playoff spot, they'll be one of the best stories in October. If not, this season could all be for naught.
-MP
13. Texas Rangers
All of a sudden, the Rangers find themselves back in control of the AL West and home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs. Of course, that says more about the West than it does about Texas; this is still a .500 team, one without a ton of depth on either side of the ball. The interesting thing, though, is that this lineup has finally started to show signs of life of late. Take care of business against the Twins and Mets this week, and no one’s going to want to face a team with Jacob deGrom and Nathan Eovaldi in the rotation plus an offense featuring Corey Seager, Wyatt Langford and Josh Jung.
-CL
12. Pittsburgh Pirates
The narrative Pirates fans are spinning these days is the same web every National League non-playoff team will get caught in this week; if only we played in the American League! Yes, the disparity between leagues is easy to blame for the Pirates shortcomings, but the front office also fell short in acquiring bullpen arms last winter, which could've kept Pittsburgh from blowing an extraordinary number of leads in the season's first half. That'll haunt these Pirates forever.
-MP
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
It's not Arizona's fault that their primary competition for a Wild Card spot, San Diego, has become one of the hottest teams in baseball over the last few weeks. Either way, though, Arizona has simply run out of bullets, especially in a rotation that hasn't gotten the boost from Corbin Burnes' return that they were hoping for. Eduardo Rodriguez has turned back into a pumpkin, and there's just not enough depth to keep pace with what's become a beast of an NL playoff chase.
–CL
10. Cleveland Guardians
Here we go again with the Guardians. Cleveland is a legitimate threat in a weak American League. Much like last season, the Guards are taking advantage of a fellow contender floundering down the stretch. This is when Cleveland plays its best baseball, so it should be no surprise they've won five straight games heading into Monday's potential postseason preview against the Red Sox.
-MP
9. Boston Red Sox
Dropping consecutive series to the Rangers and Rays won’t do much to Boston’s postseason outlook — they’ve been more or less locked into a Wild Card series in the Bronx for a while now — but it still doesn’t inspire confidence in this team’s ability to make a run come October. This offense is once again mired in a power outage, and while getting Willson Contreras and others back from the IL figures to help, who knows when that might actually be. And there’s still just a real dearth of power here that even this pitching staff might not be able to make up for.
–CL
8. Philadelphia Phillies
I don’t know what to think of the Philadelphia Phillies. On one hand, a rotation led by Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sanchez, a healthy Jesus Luzardo, a rejuvenated Aaron Nola and a much-improved Andrew Painter should will them to wins. On the other hand, Luzardo is not healthy, the lineup is top-heavy and the bullpen, outside of Jhoan Duran, is an utter disaster. The Phillies are almost certainly going to make the playoffs, but their losses in New York this week ruined any last hope they had at a division title. And with how they’re playing right now, I don’t know if I’d pick them to get beyond the Wild Card Round.
–ZR
7. Chicago Cubs
The Cubs playoff parade was put on hold Sunday as Alex Bregman was struck in the face by a foul ball. Bregman was taken to the local hospital, and it's unclear how much time he will miss as of this writing. Chicago's postseason hopes may hang in the balance, as their one clear advantage over every other NL team is their lineup. The Cubs have scored the most runs in baseball this year.
-MP
6. San Diego Padres
Yes, the schedule has helped, particularly series against Miami, Colorado, Washington, San Francisco and Cincinnati. But no matter who they've played, the Padres look like a different team from the one we saw for much of the year, with their big bats finally mashing and their rotation coming into focus with Nick Pivetta now back in the fold. San Diego is now dead even with Chicago and Philly in the Wild Card race, and no one will want to face this lineup and this bullpen in a short series.
–CL
5. New York Yankees
Just when it seemed like New York was getting ready to make a move, with Aaron Judge finally back in the lineup after months on the shelf, the reigning AL MVP landed right back on the IL — this time with a calf strain that could well jeopardize his entire postseason. It’s been that sort of year for the Yankees, which have the pitching to keep believing in them as contenders but just haven’t been able to put it all together enough to take command of their own playoff destiny. And with a Judge-less offense and a penchant for mistake-filled baseball, winning three series in a row feels like a tough ask even in this AL.
–CL
4. Atlanta Braves
The Atlanta Braves punched their ticket to the playoffs this week, and thanks to the Phillies’ struggles, they’re on the cusp of winning the NL East — ensuring a top-three seed in the National League. Tyler Mahle pitched another gem, and Ronald Acuña Jr. is hitting his stride at the perfect time. There’re still some concerns with the team, like the No. 3 spot in their rotation and struggling stars like Austin Riley and Ozzie Albies, but getting to the playoffs is a big deal, and the Braves can take pride in checking that box.
–ZR
3. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays may well have sewn up the AL East this week, taking two of three from the Red Sox over the weekend to stretch their lead over the Yankees ahead of an all-important four-game set in the Bronx beginning on Tuesday. Even if New York were to sweep all four, though, Tampa would still have the inside track to the division and the No. 1 overall seed. This pitching staff continues to thrive beyond all expectation even with some recent injuries, and the hitting has done just enough. Whether that recipe will withstand the postseason is the only question now.
–CL
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Don't look now, but L.A.'s lineup has begun to stir, with Kyle Tucker looking like the player the Dodgers thought they were paying for this offseason. They also got Edwin Diaz back this week, and he's suddenly looking like the star closer of old — potentially answering this team's biggest question entering October. We know the rotation will be there; if they have Tucker at the height of his powers and a one-two punch in Diaz and Tanner Scott at the end of games, the three-peat march might be back on.
–CL
1. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers set a franchise record with 98 wins on Sunday. They still have a full week to go to add to that mark, and appear likely to reach the 100-win plateau. That's a great accomplishment, but it won't mean squat if Milwaukee falls to the Los Angeles Dodgers — or any other NL team for that matter — on their way to that elusive NL pennant. The Brewers are the favorites, but the Dodgers are lingering right behind them.
-MP

item.content:encoded:
Mike Trout has spent his entire MLB career with the Los Angeles Angels, going from the first overall pick in the draft to one of the most recognisable stars in baseball. That career has been mirrored by his financial profile, with the bulk of his publicly known earnings from football coming through long-term contracts.
Trout is still under the massive extension he signed with the Los Angeles Angels in 2019 through 2026. The deal runs up to and including the end of the 2030 season and still pays a healthy annual salary, with his commercial relationships and investment interests providing other sources of income.
Mike Trout net worth and Los Angeles Angels earnings
Public estimates vary regarding Mike Trout's net worth because private investments, taxes, spending and other personal assets are not fully disclosed. Reports estimating Trout’s net worth at around $220 million in 2026 have cited Celebrity Net Worth. That figure should be viewed as an estimate, not an independently audited accounting of his assets.
That wealth stems from Trout’s MLB pay. Celebrity Net Worth reports Spotrac listing his 2026 cash salary at $35.45 million, but his payroll figure is about $37.12 million because of contract accounting. His 2019 extension is for $426.5 million over 12 years with an average annual value of roughly $35.54 million.
| Financial category | Mike Trout in 2026 |
| Estimated net worth | $220 million |
| 2026 cash salary | $35.45 million |
| 2026 payroll figure | $37.12 million |
| Major contract | 12 years, $426.5 million |
| Contract through | 2030 |
| Average annual value | $35.54 million |
Mike Trout’s historic contract remains his financial foundation
The centrepiece to Trout’s earning power in MLB is his current 12-year, $426.5 million deal with the Los Angeles Angels. The deal was done in March 2019 and extends through the 2030 season, providing Trout with guaranteed long-term financial security with the organization. It also features a full no-trade clause and no opt-outs.
The deal comes with a $35.45 million cash salary for 2026. Spotrac’s contract breakdown reveals the same $35.45 million base figure for every year through 2030, while the payroll value is closer to $37.12 million each season because of the allocation of his signing bonus.
Trout’s total MLB cash earnings have also reached a milestone. Based on those figures, his cash earnings through 2026 are roughly $338.64 million. Spotrac lists his career earnings through the 2025 season at $303.19 million, and his 2026 salary at another $35.45 million.
| Contract detail | Amount |
| Total contract | $426.5 million |
| Contract length | 12 years |
| 2026 base cash salary | $35.45 million |
| 2026 payroll value | $37.12 million |
| Contract end | 2030 |
| Estimated cash earnings through 2026 | $338.64 million |
Mike Trout endorsements and investments add off-field wealth
Trout’s earning power goes beyond his Los Angeles Angels salary through a portfolio of commercial partnerships developed during his MLB career. One of his biggest brand relationships has been with Nike, which has previously given Trout a signature shoe line. His perennial baseball star status has also made him attractive to companies across sports, fitness and consumer markets.
Another important chapter in the financial history of Trout is BODYARMOR. Trout was an investor and ambassador for the sports-drink brand, as was Kobe Bryant, an early major shareholder. In 2018, Coca-Cola Company acquired a minority stake in BODYARMOR and in 2021 announced it would buy the remaining 85% for $5.6 billion. Public accounts have linked Trout to the firm’s original cohort of investors, although the exact amount of his personal earnings has not been publicly disclosed.
Mike Trout’s overall financial picture for 2026 largely hinges on his long-term deal with the Los Angeles Angels and an estimated $338 million in MLB cash earnings through the 2026 season, with his wealth outside of baseball buoyed by endorsements and investments.

item.title: [FanGraphs] Bobby Witt Jr. and the Off-Peak MVP Season
item.dc:creator: Davy Andrews
item.description: Bobby Witt Jr. is having a down year. He’s running his worst batting line in three seasons. He’s in danger of missing the 20-homer threshold for the first time in his career. A lower back injury in July will also limit him to a career low in games played. Put it together, and Witt is on pace to put up his the lowest WAR total since his 5.9-win 2023 campaign. Oh, and he also grabbed hold of the American League lead in WAR back in July and still hasn’t relinquished it. A down year by Bobby Witt Jr
item.content:encoded:
Bobby Witt Jr. is having a down year. He’s running his worst batting line in three seasons. He’s in danger of missing the 20-homer threshold for the first time in his career. A lower back injury in July will also limit him to a career low in games played. Put it together, and Witt is on pace to put up his the lowest WAR total since his 5.9-win 2023 campaign. Oh, and he also grabbed hold of the American League lead in WAR back in July and still hasn’t relinquished it. A down year by Bobby Witt Jr.’s standards is still good enough to make him a deserving MVP.
I don’t know if Witt is going to win his first MVP this year. Ours is the only flavor of WAR in which he leads the AL, and he leads by just a quarter of a win. He ranks third by Baseball Reference’s rWAR and is eighth by Baseball Prospectus’ WARP. Yordan Alvarez leads all of baseball in WARP because he’s hitting like, well, Yordan Alvarez and staying healthy like, well, someone other than Yordan Alvarez. Cam Schlittler leads the AL in Baseball Reference WAR, and he’s been so dominant that he deserves consideration for the Cy Young-MVP combo — if only he’d pitched just 23 fewer innings last year, he could’ve gone for the trifecta with Rookie of the Year. Kevin McGonigle has played like an MVP from the moment he arrived in Detroit, and Junior Caminero has surpassed 40 home runs for the second season in a row as a 23-year-old. All of these guys have a case, and they aren’t the only ones who merit inclusion in the discussion:
| Name | fWAR Rk | fWAR | rWAR Rk | rWAR | WARP Rk | WARP | Avg Rk | Avg WAR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bobby Witt Jr. | 1 | 6.6 | 3 | 6.5 | 8 | 5 | 4 | 6.0 |
| Yordan Alvarez | 2 | 6.4 | 4 | 6.4 | 1 | 7.3 | 2 | 6.7 |
| Cam Schlittler | 3 | 6.1 | 1 | 7 | 3 | 5.8 | 2 | 6.3 |
| Dylan Cease | 4 | 5.5 | 8 | 5.7 | 12 | 4.6 | 8 | 5.3 |
| Miguel Vargas | 5 | 5.2 | 10 | 5.3 | 2 | 5.9 | 6 | 5.5 |
| Junior Caminero | 6 | 5.2 | 7 | 5.7 | 5 | 5.3 | 6 | 5.4 |
| Kevin McGonigle | 7 | 5.1 | 2 | 6.7 | 4 | 5.3 | 4 | 5.7 |
| Randy Arozarena | 8 | 5.1 | 11 | 5.3 | 16 | 4 | 12 | 4.8 |
| Dillon Dingler | 9 | 4.6 | 25 | 4 | 23 | 3.3 | 19 | 4.0 |
| Drew Rasmussen | 10 | 4.6 | 21 | 4.2 | 13 | 4.4 | 15 | 4.4 |
| Reid Detmers | 11 | 4.6 | 35 | 3.7 | 11 | 4.7 | 19 | 4.3 |
| Parker Messick | 13 | 4.6 | 6 | 5.8 | 9 | 4.8 | 9 | 5.1 |
| Pete Alonso | 14 | 4.2 | 18 | 4.3 | 6 | 5.3 | 13 | 4.6 |
| Ceddanne Rafaela | 21 | 3.9 | 9 | 5.4 | 94 | 1.7 | 41 | 3.7 |
| Gavin Williams | 27 | 3.7 | 46 | 3.1 | 7 | 5.2 | 27 | 4.0 |
| Wilyer Abreu | 32 | 3.4 | 5 | 5.8 | 20 | 3.6 | 19 | 4.3 |
| Mike Trout | 40 | 3.2 | 28 | 3.9 | 10 | 4.8 | 26 | 4.0 |
Pete Crow-Armstrong, Jacob Misiorowski, Schlittler, McGonigle and JJ Wetherholt have made the AL MVP the only major award that’s really in question). If you want to read a particularly good example, you should check out the one Mario Delgado Genzor wrote for Baseball Prospectus on Friday. I want to focus on something slightly different — namely, how good Witt has already been in years when he missed out on an MVP and how unusual it would be for him to win it this year.
(A quick note before we get into it: We’re about to spend a lot of time talking about WAR. I know I mentioned rWAR and WARP earlier. They’re an important piece of the puzzle, especially due to the outsized effect rWAR in particular has on the MVP conversation, but from here on out, we’re sticking with good old FanGraphs WAR.)
This is Witt’s fifth major league season, and you could argue that it’s his fourth consecutive MVP-caliber campaign. Mind you, that argument would focus only on 2022, in which he put up 5.9 WAR, good for 10th in the majors. There’s no argument to be had about the 2024 and 2025 seasons. That said, along with Shohei Ohtani’s combined 9.2-WAR 2022 sesaon, they are the two most valuable seasons this decade for which a position player did not win an MVP. In 2024, Witt ran a 169 wRC+, stole 31 bases, and put up a Fielding Run Value of 11, fourth among all shortstops. That was good for 10.5 WAR, and it took the best season of Aaron Judge’s career – 58 home runs, a 19% walk rate, and a .322 batting average – to beat him. In 2025, Witt put up 8.0 WAR with a 130 wRC+, 38 steals, and 20 FRV, the best mark among all shortstops. Again, he was bested by a 10-win season from Judge and Cal Raleigh’s 60-homer campaign. Witt has never received a first place MVP vote.
Crow-Armstrong, who has the National League MVP all but locked down, gives us a great example of what it normally takes to win an MVP award. He may even finish with 10.5 WAR through his excellence in all three phases of the game, just like Witt did in 2024. Players like Judge, Ohtani, and Mike Trout, whose base level of talent is so high that a healthy campaign is almost sure to keep them a step above the rest of the league, don’t come around all that often. Even when they do come around, they still need to be playing at something close to their peak, and peaks don’t last that long. Until Ohtani, the only player to win more than three MVPs was Barry Bonds, whose regimen for raising and widening his peak has been well documented. Sometimes that’s because of voter fatigue, but often it’s because somebody else popped up with an amazing, undeniable season like PCA’s. Most of the time, the MVP is an already great player for whom everything goes perfectly. They stay healthy and they play not just their best, but over their heads. Think of Ronald Acuña Jr. winning the NL MVP in 2023 with 9.1 WAR, 4.1 more than his next-best total, or Mookie Betts winning the AL MVP in 2018 with 10.2 WAR, 2.8 more than his next-best total.
Generally speaking, since the voting started getting more rigorous in the last couple decades, those are the two categories of players who win MVPs. We see all-time greats who perform like only they are capable of performing, and we see excellent players who put it all together in a blaze of glory. Witt’s 2024 season probably falls into that second category. He wasn’t quite at his defensive or baserunning peak, but he put up his best season at the plate by nearly 40 points of wRC+ and DRC+, and he ended up with an all-timer of a season. His 10.5 WAR tied for the 36th-best position player campaign of all time. His company? Willie Mays and Babe Ruth twice apiece, Barry Bonds, and Rogers Hornsby. Unfortunately, he ran into one of those special players from the first category, in the form of Judge. If Witt had put up those 2024 numbers this year, he’d be en route to a unanimous MVP just like PCA.
But I said “in theory” earlier, and I said it because Witt isn’t done yet. He’s still just 26, and if not for those weeks he missed with back tightness, or a wOBA that’s more than 30 points below his xwOBA, he’d now be wrapping up his third straight seven-plus-win season. He’s elite in every facet of the game and he doesn’t look like he’s in danger of slowing down any time soon. It wouldn’t be much of a shock to see him rediscover his nine- or 10-win form. In other words, there’s at least a chance Witt belongs to that first category of player and not the second.
Earlier I mentioned Acuña and Betts claiming MVPs by putting up the best years of their careers by a long shot. That’s pretty standard. Especially in recent years, it’s awfully rare for a player to take home an MVP award in something other than the best season of their career, unless they also won the MVP in the best year of their career. Leaving those multi-time MVPs out (and excluding 2020 for obvious reasons), here’s the whole list of players who won an MVP in a year that wasn’t their best by fWAR since 2011: Giancarlo Stanton and Paul Goldschmidt.
Goldschmidt put up 6.8 WAR in his 2022 NL MVP season and 7.2 in 2015. In that sense, Goldschmidt fit a third archetype: the established star who doesn’t put up their biggest WAR total, and instead wins MVP as something of a career achievement award. Stanton put up 6.5 WAR in 2017, not quite the 6.8-win campaign he put up in 2014, but he was facing a weaker field, he was more established as a star, and he had the cachet of a 59-homer season. We’re talking about gaps of less than half a win. We had some multi-time winners, but Acuña, Betts, Cody Bellinger, Christian Yelich, Jose Altuve, Kris Bryant, Josh Donaldson, Andrew McCutchen, and Buster Posey all won MVP in the best seasons of their career by fWAR.
Let’s say that Witt does win the MVP this year. For the sake of round numbers, let’s say he closes strong and finishes with 7.0 WAR. That would be just the third-best season of his career, and a full 3.5 WAR below his career-high. Baseball Reference lists MVP winners going back to 1911, and in that time, Witt would become just the ninth position player to win MVP in a season that trailed their best year by such a wide margin. The list of players to do it before him is full of three-time MVPs like Joe DiMaggio, Mickey Mantle, and Mike Schmidt. Not only that, but you’ll note that if Witt does make this list, the only higher number in either column will belong to Mantle:
| Player | MVP Year | MVP WAR | Best Year | Best WAR | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frankie Frisch | 1931 | 4.1 | 1927 | 9.7 | 5.6 |
| Mickey Mantle | 1962 | 6.0 | 1956 | 11.5 | 5.5 |
| Willie Stargell | 1979 | 2.7 | 1971 | 8.2 | 5.4 |
| Joe DiMaggio | 1947 | 4.8 | 1941 | 9.7 | 4.9 |
| Freddie Freeman | 2020* | 3.0 | 2023 | 7.7 | 4.7 |
| Robin Yount | 1989 | 5.3 | 1982 | 9.8 | 4.5 |
| Andre Dawson | 1987 | 3.5 | 1982 | 7.3 | 3.8 |
| Mike Schmidt | 1986 | 5.8 | 1974 | 9.4 | 3.6 |
| Roger Peckinpaugh | 1925 | 2.4 | 1919 | 5.9 | 3.5 |
The last person to do so was Robin Yount, who won the AL MVP with 9.8 WAR in 1982, and then again with 5.3 WAR in 1989, long before anybody knew that Total Zone considered him the 11th-worst defender in the majors. This hasn’t happened in nearly 30 years, and Witt is in a very different boat here. He’s not one of the two MVP favorites because his season looks great to the eye but doesn’t fool the advanced metrics. He’s not an aging star who can count on some lifetime-achievement votes. He’s a young gun who’s leading his league in WAR because he excels in every facet of the game.
I realize that this is far from the most meticulous analysis I’ve ever conducted, and that MVP voting is and should be about more than WAR. Still, I hope I’ve put this season in the context it deserves. By our measuring stick, Witt has been the best player in the American League this season. He’s done so despite missing time due to injury. He’s done so despite some bad batted ball luck. And he’s done so despite not even coming close to the highest gear we know he’s got available to him, because that gear is so high that it’s normally reserved for inner-circle Hall of Famers. However the voting goes, Witt’s been in MVP form for three or four years now.
Davy Andrews is a Brooklyn-based musician and a writer at FanGraphs. He can be found on Bluesky @davyandrewsdavy.bsky.social.

item.title: [timesofindia.indiatimes.com] Inspiring story of the day: José Ramírez grew up playing with a glove that was too small and was ignored by MLB scouts; years later he reached 1,000 career RBIs
item.dc:creator: Global Sports Desk
item.description: Some baseball dreams begin with the finest equipment, elite coaching and scouts waiting to spot the next big star. José Ramírez's journey began very differently. The Cleveland Guardians star grew up with limited resources, faced doubts about his potential and had to fight for recognition. Years later, he reached 1,000 career RBIs, turning an overlooked beginning into a remarkable MLB story. José Ramírez's humble beginnings in the Dominican Republic Long before thousands of fans cheered his name
item.content:encoded:
Some baseball dreams begin with the finest equipment, elite coaching and scouts waiting to spot the next big star. José Ramírez's journey began very differently. The Cleveland Guardians star grew up with limited resources, faced doubts about his potential and had to fight for recognition. Years later, he reached 1,000 career RBIs, turning an overlooked beginning into a remarkable MLB story.
José Ramírez's humble beginnings in the Dominican Republic
Long before thousands of fans cheered his name at Progressive Field, Ramírez was a young boy in Baní, a city in the Dominican Republic, trying to make the most of whatever baseball equipment he could find.
His family faced financial struggles, and even getting a proper glove was difficult. In a 2023 MLB feature, Ramírez recalled the challenges his family faced while he was growing up.
“It was difficult for my dad,” he said through interpreter Agustin Rivero. “He didn’t have much work, we didn’t have much money. I had to play with a glove that was too tight.”
That small detail offers a glimpse into the reality of Ramírez's early life. For him, baseball was never simply a game played for fun. It represented a chance to change his family's circumstances and build a future beyond the financial limits he knew as a child.
Before he began playing organised baseball, Ramírez and other neighbourhood children played Vitilla, a popular Dominican street game. They used plastic water jug caps as balls and sticks as bats. The makeshift equipment could not match what elite prospects used, but the children made the most of what they had.
Ramírez also faced a challenge that had nothing to do with money. His small frame made him easy to overlook in a sport where scouts often search for size, strength and physical potential.
Yet, the young infielder kept showing up and competing. His story was taking shape long before a Major League Baseball team gave him a chance.
MLB scouts overlooked José Ramírez despite his talent
Ramírez's road to professional baseball was anything but straightforward. While other young players attracted attention at showcases in the Dominican Republic, he often found himself waiting on the sidelines.
By the time he was 17, his chances of securing a professional contract appeared to be slipping away. Many of the top Dominican prospects signed with MLB teams at 16, leaving Ramírez behind as scouts focused on younger players with more conventional physical profiles.
He was frequently used as a fill-in at showcases rather than receiving the same opportunities as the headline prospects. His lack of size and limited scouting attention made it harder for him to stand out, even when his performance suggested he deserved a closer look.
Ramírez later described the doubts he faced in an ESPN interview, recalling how people judged him before he had the chance to prove himself.
“I knew it would be hard for me [to get signed] because [scouts] are always looking for a Mike Trout, a Bryce Harper. Those kind of guys; big, strong guys. I imagine that [José] Altuve had the same thing happen to him. I guess nobody believed Altuve could be what he has become. Sometimes your size, a smaller body, one does not attract attention or anything and nobody believes in you,” he said.
The lack of interest could have ended his dream before it truly began. Instead, Ramírez continued to play, trusting his ability even when the people evaluating him did not share that confidence.
His opportunity finally arrived in 2009. During a showcase, Cleveland's scouting director John Mirabelli and scout Ramón Peña watched him play second base. Ramírez delivered three hits that day, followed by three more the next day and five hits during a doubleheader.
Peña pushed for Cleveland to sign him. The Guardians' organisation, then known as the Indians, eventually offered Ramírez a $50,000 signing bonus.
It was a modest investment compared with the money given to highly sought-after international prospects. But that decision would become one of the most significant signings in the franchise's history.
José Ramírez turned a modest signing into an MLB career
Even after signing with Cleveland, Ramírez had no guarantee of becoming a major league star. His small signing bonus did not bring the same expectations or opportunities that came with a lucrative prospect contract.
He had to earn his place at every level, moving through the Dominican Summer League, the Arizona Rookie League and several other Minor League stops. There were no shortcuts. Each promotion required him to prove that his performance could translate against stronger competition.
Cleveland's front office later acknowledged that Ramírez did not arrive with the attention usually reserved for elite prospects. His progress came through steady work rather than early hype.
That gradual rise makes his career particularly striking. Ramírez developed into one of baseball's most consistent hitters, combining contact skills, speed, power and versatility. He also became a switch-hitter capable of putting pressure on opposing pitchers from either side of the plate.
His success challenged the assumptions that had limited his opportunities as a teenager. The traits that once made him easy to overlook did not prevent him from becoming a central figure in Cleveland's lineup.
Over time, Ramírez became far more than a promising player who exceeded expectations. He established himself as a franchise cornerstone, a perennial offensive threat and a player whose contributions extended well beyond individual statistics.
The journey also reflects the importance of the people who believed in him early. Peña continued to advocate for Ramírez when others saw little reason to invest in him. That faith gave the young Dominican infielder an opening, but Ramírez still had to turn it into a career.
José Ramírez reaches 1,000 career RBIs with the Guardians
On September 18, 2026, Ramírez added another defining moment to his career. The Guardians star crushed a solo home run against the Athletics at Progressive Field, recording his 1,000th career RBI during Cleveland's 5-3 victory.
The milestone came in the sixth inning, with his 401-foot blast giving the home crowd another reason to celebrate a player who had spent years earning their admiration.
Ramírez became just the second player in Cleveland franchise history to reach 1,000 RBIs, joining Earl Averill. He also became the 12th active MLB player to reach the mark.
For a player who once struggled to attract the attention of scouts, the achievement carries a special meaning. It reflects years of consistency, development and the ability to deliver when his team needs him.
Guardians manager Stephen Vogt captured the scale of the accomplishment by putting it in perspective.
“I like to use those round numbers,” Vogt said. “[It’s] 10 years of 100 RBIs. When you break it down that way, it's incredible what he has accomplished, and he's not even close to being done, right?”
Ramírez, however, remained focused on the team's success rather than his personal achievement.
“Thank God for the opportunity to play here for this organization and be able to achieve [1,000 RBIs],” Ramírez said through team interpreter Agustin Rivero. “But most important is that we're able to win today, because you guys know what I really want to do here, which is win.”
That mindset helps explain why Ramírez's story resonates beyond the milestone itself. His journey is about more than proving scouts wrong. It is about turning a difficult start into a career built on persistence, consistency and loyalty to the game.
From a young boy playing with an ill-fitting glove in Baní to one of Cleveland's most accomplished hitters, José Ramírez has shown that a player's beginning does not have to define his ceiling. His 1,000th RBI is another chapter in a story that is still being written.
Reporting note: The career milestone and game details are based on MLB's September 19, 2026, report. The early-life details are drawn from MLB's 2023 profile and ESPN's reporting on Ramírez's rise.

item.content:encoded:
There hasn't been much for New York Mets fans to get excited about in 2026. But on Friday night, Mets outfielder Juan Soto accomplished a feat that only three other superstars have done in MLB history.
Soto launched a 428-foot three-run blast in New York's 6-3 win over the Philadelphia Phillies on Friday. Despite dealing with injuries this season, the lefty-swinging slugger now has 26 home runs in 103 games. This was also the 27-year-old's 270th homer in the majors. That's noteworthy because the five-time All-Star is now one of just four players to reach 270 home runs and 100 stolen bases before their 28th birthday, according to MLB.com's Sarah Langs.
The other stars on this list include Hall of Famer Ken Griffey Jr. and a pair of three-time MVPs in Alex Rodriguez and Mike Trout. All four players in this exclusive group were playing in the big leagues at 19. And with Soto wrapping up just the second season of his 15-year contract with the Mets, New York fans should get to see the talented outfielder make more history for the foreseeable future.
What's next for Juan Soto and the Mets in 2027?
Heading into the 2026 season, several pundits thought the Mets could compete for the top spot in the National League East. Instead, New York is currently in last place in the NL East at 70-84. But it's not all doom and gloom for the Mets beyond this year's campaign.
In addition to Soto continuing to play like a star while healthy, some of New York's talented prospects have emerged as potential key pieces to the team's future. Starting pitcher Nolan McLean and outfielder Carson Benge should receive some National League Rookie of the Year votes this year, and outfielder A.J. Ewing has turned heads by reaching the majors after starting 2026 at Double-A. The Mets also revamped their farm system at the trade deadline, most notably acquiring the team's new No. 1 prospect, infielder Jefferson Rojas.
New York is expected to be a major spender in the offseason as well. Owner Steve Cohen could make an aggressive offer for left-handed ace Tarik Skubal, while also targeting other top free agents. Either way, with the 2026 season almost in the rearview mirror for the Mets, many fans will be waiting to see if the team can bounce back in 2027.
Justin Binkowski is a lifelong baseball fan returning to cover the sport he loves after spending nearly a decade writing about video games. Before his time as managing editor at Dot Esports, Binkowski attended King's College in Wilkes-Barre, PA, where he was also a relief pitcher on the school's baseball team. While in college, Binkowski was a media relations intern for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders during the 2014 season.

item.dc:creator: Ryan Lewis
item.description: As Guardians chase playoff spot, Jose Ramirez records career RBI 1,000 CLEVELAND — Cleveland’s baseball franchise has never had a player quite like Jose Ramirez. Along with signing under-market contracts to remain with the Guardians twice and the many memorable moments in a Cleveland uniform over the past decade-plus, his assault on the record books added another chapter Sept. 18 in a 5-3 win over the Athletics, which allowed them to retake the lead in the American League Central race with eight
item.content:encoded:
As Guardians chase playoff spot, Jose Ramirez records career RBI 1,000
CLEVELAND — Cleveland’s baseball franchise has never had a player quite like Jose Ramirez.
Along with signing under-market contracts to remain with the Guardians twice and the many memorable moments in a Cleveland uniform over the past decade-plus, his assault on the record books added another chapter Sept. 18 in a 5-3 win over the Athletics, which allowed them to retake the lead in the American League Central race with eight game remaining.
In that win, Ramirez went 2-for-5 with a home run and two RBIs, which gave him 1,000 RBIs in his career. In doing so, he became the 12th active player to reach 1,000 RBIs, joining Freddie Freeman, Paul Goldschmidt, Manny Machado, Giancarlo Stanton, Mike Trout, Bryce Harper, Nolan Arenado, Andrew McCutchen, Salvador Perez, Eugenio Suarez and Carlos Santana.
“Very important to thank God for that opportunity to play here in this organization and to be bale to achieve that,” Ramirez said through a team translator. “But the most important part is that we’re able to win today because you guys know what I really want to do here, which is win.”
Jose Ramirez stats
He’s also just the second Cleveland player to hit that milestone with the franchise, joining Earl Averill (1,084), whose playing career ended in the early 1940s.
It’s a significant line on Ramirez's Hall of Fame resume. The home run also brought him within three of becoming only the ninth player in MLB history to reach the 300/300 club for home runs and stolen bases.
“I like to use round numbers,” Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said. “It’s 10 years of 100 RBIs. When you break it down that way, it’s incredible what he has accomplished, and he’s not even close to being done. And very few people get do it, and it’s really cool to be here to watch it.”
It was a milestone night for Ramirez, though it came at the end of what has been one of his more frustrating seasons, particularly over the last few weeks while he’s played through hamate been surgery rehab.
Jose Ramirez injury update
He’s posted a 90 wRC+, which would be the first time since he became a full-time player in 2016 he’s been below 100 (league average). Since he returned to the lineup on July 22, after the procedure, he’s hit .216 with a .567 OPS.
“I keep working on it every day,” Ramirez said. “I have to keep working in the training room every day because this type of injury is the type where one day you feel good, the next you don’t feel so well, but you have to keep grinding.”
Despite the lack of his usual MVP-caliber production on a nightly basis, Vogt and the Guardians have still applauded the way Ramirez has fought through the situation. It’s one of the attributes that often gets mentioned first when listing why they feel he’s so valuable to the organization.
“Even as he was coming back and we have to give him off days, he was not happy about it,” Vogt said. “He wants to play every day. He wants to give us everything that he has on any given day. We know that there’s days where he’s not feeling good and he still goes out and gives 100 percent of what he has that day.
“It’s such a great example for our young guys to see that just because you’re not feeling 100 percent, it doesn’t mean you can’t go out and compete and contribute to help the team win.”
Ryan Lewis covers the Guardians for the Beacon Journal. He can be reached at rlewis1@gannett.com.

item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND -- As the Progressive Field crowd roared around him, José Ramírez paused and leaned back in the left-handed batter’s box to admire his work. There was no doubt where the baseball he launched to right field was headed.
That image has played on repeat over the past 14 seasons. This time, it came with a heavy dose of history, and it was well-timed as the Guardians continue to push for the postseason.
Ramírez tallied his 1,000th career RBI on Friday by launching his 297th career home run, in the sixth inning of the Guardians’ matchup with the A’s in the opener of a three-game series. The superstar third baseman joined Earl Averill (1,084) as the only players in Cleveland franchise history to hit the RBI milestone.
The Guardians improved to 79-75 with their third straight win. They entered Friday with the same record as the White Sox, but Chicago technically led the division because it holds the tiebreaker over Cleveland after winning the season series.
It means the Guardians must finish with more wins than the Sox to win the Central for a third straight year. Ramírez helped; his towering blast went a Statcast-projected 401 feet and had a 102.4 mph exit velocity.
Ramírez, who turned 34 years old on Thursday, is now just the 12th active player with 1,000 career RBIs, joining Freddie Freeman, Paul Goldschmidt, Nolan Arenado, Manny Machado, Giancarlo Stanton, Andrew McCutchen, Carlos Santana, Bryce Harper, Salvador Perez, Mike Trout and Eugenio Suárez.
The home run was Ramírez’s first since Aug. 30 and just his 12th this season. He entered Friday with an uncharacteristic .683 OPS in 117 games, in an injury-impacted campaign after he missed five weeks following left hamate surgery.
Ramírez has been dealt with the effects of that procedure since he came off the injured list on July 22. On Friday, he reminded us he’s always just one swing away from impacting a game in a big way.
